latin.545: GAR. Respondeo 1. Aliud est si dicas simpliciter aliquem peccare, aliud si dicas aliquem in alio peccavisse. Nam illud sane ex vi vocis non significat imputationem peccati, sed hoc posterius designat imputationem. Quomodo enim qui multis post saeculis exstiterunt, dici possunt iam antea in alio peccasse, nisi quia ille eorum actum exercuit, & qui posterorum ita reputatur, ac si ipsi illum commisissent?
latin.546: Sic satisfacere aliquem, & alicui satisfactionem imputari, sunt sane longe diversa, & tamen cum docent Theologi nos in Christo satisfecisse, non aliud sibi volunt, quam Christi satisfactionem nobis imputari, sive Christum eam satisfactionem exhibuisse, quae propter unionem, quam cum eo habemus tanquam capite nostro spirituali & mystico, nobis imputetur, ita ut apud Deum habeamur, quasi ipsi per nos satisfecissemus.
latin.547: PLAC. Primum, non dicit Scriptura nos in Adamo peccasse. Deinde, non video cur illa locutio vim significet imputationem, qua peccatum alienum, nempe Adami, fiat aut existat nostrum. Dicimur enim mori in Adamo, nec tamen mors Adami nobis imputatur.
latin.548: Dici possumus in Adamo creati fuisse, creati fuisse iusti & beati, eiecti fuisse e paradiso &c., nec tamen eius creatio, aut iustitia originalis, aut eiectio e paradiso nobis imputatur. Potuimus ergo dici in eo peccasse, quomodo dici possumus in eo fuisse, quia ille quam naturam tam peccatum suum nobiscum communicavit propagatione naturali.
latin.549: Ad satisfactionem Christi quod attinet, cum dicimur in Christo satisfecisse, nihil aliud intelligi mihi videtur, nisi Christum loco nostro pro nobis satisfecisse: num igitur similiter Adamus loco nostro pro nobis peccavit? Tenebamur pro se quisque satisfacere. Id erat nobis impossibile. Christus, qui non tenebatur, vadem nostrum sese constituit, & pro nobis satisfecit. Potestne idem de nobis & Adamo dici? Tenebamurne peccare? num sese Adamus vadem nostrum constituit, ut pro nobis peccaret?
latin.550: Peto etiam, quando in Christo satisfecimus? opinor quando passus est. Num igitur tunc nobis imputata est Christi satisfactio? Tunc igitur fuimus iustificati, nondum existentes, nondum credentes. Non ergo per fidem sumus iustificati, quandoquidem iustificatio nostra tanto nostram & existentiam & fidem antecessit. Adde quod unionem cum Christo tanquam capite nostro spirituali & mystico non habemus nisi per fidem, sequitur ergo fidem nostram imputatio satisfactionis Christi seu iustificatio nostra. Quid est cur non dicamus similiter nos unionem non habere cum Adamo tanquam capite peccatorum, nisi per vitium haereditarium, quo suum nobiscum peccatum communicavit. Itaque posteriorem esse eo vitio peccati Adamici imputationem.

pass_a.545: GAR's first reply: bare 'someone sins' is not the same as 'someone sinned in another.' Only the second marks imputation. How else could later ages be said to have already sinned in another, unless he did their act and they are counted as if they had done it?
pass_a.546: Satisfying and having satisfaction imputed are far apart. Yet when theologians say we satisfied in Christ they mean only that his satisfaction is imputed through union with him as spiritual head, so God reckons us as if we had satisfied.
pass_a.547: Placeus: Scripture never says we sinned in Adam. Nor does 'in Adam' talk force an imputation that makes his alien act ours. We die in Adam, yet his death is not imputed.
pass_a.548: We may be said created, just, blessed, or cast from paradise in Adam without those acts being imputed. So 'sinned in him' can mean only that he passed nature and sin to us by natural generation.
pass_a.549: 'Satisfied in Christ' means Christ satisfied in our stead as surety—each of us owed satisfaction and could not pay it, so he became our bondsman. Adam is no parallel: we were never bound to sin, nor did he stand surety that he might sin for us in our place.
pass_a.550: If we satisfied when he suffered, was Christ's satisfaction then imputed to us so that we were justified while not yet existing and not yet believing? That would set justification before faith. Add that union with Christ as spiritual head is only by faith; therefore imputation of his satisfaction, or our justification, follows our faith. Why not say likewise that union with Adam as head of sinners is only by the hereditary vice that passed his sin to us—so the imputation of Adam's sin is later than that vice?

545: GAR. I answer 1. It is one thing if you say simply that someone sins, another if you say that someone has sinned in another. For the former, surely by force of the word, does not signify imputation of sin, but this latter designates imputation. For how can those who existed many ages afterward be said to have already before sinned in another, except because he exercised their act, and he of the posterity is so reputed, as if they themselves had committed it?
546: So for someone to satisfy, and for satisfaction to be imputed to someone, are surely far diverse. And yet when the theologians teach that we have satisfied in Christ, they mean nothing else than that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us. Or that Christ exhibited that satisfaction which, because of the union which we have with him as our spiritual and mystical head, is imputed to us, so that before God we are held as if we ourselves had satisfied through ourselves.
547: PLAC. First, Scripture does not say that we sinned in Adam. Next, I do not see why that manner of speaking should signify imputation by which another's sin, namely Adam's, becomes or exists as ours. For we are said to die in Adam, and yet Adam's death is not imputed to us.
548: We can be said to have been created in Adam, to have been created just and blessed, to have been cast out of paradise, and so on, and yet neither his creation, nor original righteousness, nor casting out of paradise is imputed to us. Therefore we could be said to have sinned in him, in the way we can be said to have been in him, because he communicated to us both his nature and his sin by natural propagation.
549: As for Christ's satisfaction, when we are said to have satisfied in Christ, nothing else seems to me to be understood, except that Christ in our place satisfied for us: did Adam therefore likewise in our place sin for us? Each of us was bound to satisfy for himself. That was impossible for us. Christ, who was not bound, constituted himself our surety, and satisfied for us. Can the same be said of us and of Adam? Were we bound to sin? Did Adam constitute himself our surety, that he might sin for us?
550: I ask also, when did we satisfy in Christ? I think when he suffered. Was Christ's satisfaction therefore then imputed to us? Then therefore we were justified, not yet existing, not yet believing. We are therefore not justified by faith, seeing that our justification so far preceded both our existence and our faith. Add that we do not have union with Christ as our spiritual and mystical head except by faith; it follows therefore that the imputation of Christ's satisfaction, or our justification, follows our faith. What reason is there why we should not similarly say that we do not have union with Adam as head of sinners except by the hereditary vice by which he communicated his sin with us? And so the imputation of Adam's sin is later than that vice.

545.choice: Simple peccare ≠ in alio peccavisse; only the latter means imputation

546.choice: Christ-satisfaction talk is imputation-via-union, offered as parallel

547.choice: No 'we sinned in Adam' text; dying in Adam ≠ Adam's death imputed

548.choice: Other in-Adam phrases without imputation; sin passed by propagation

549.choice: Christ surety for owed satisfaction; Adam not surety for owed sin

550.choice: Imputation of Christ's satisfaction follows faith-union; Adam's follows hereditary vice; tip before GAR 2
